data.title: US goods trade deficit deteriorates further as AI helps to lift imports to record high
data.description:
WASHINGTON — The US trade deficit in goods widened sharply in October as an AI infrastructure buildout boosted imports to a record high, potentially putting trade on course to again subtract from economic growth in the fourth quarter.

The surge in imports reported by the Commerce Department on Friday (Nov 27) was also across other categories, including motor vehicles, industrial supplies and consumer goods, reflecting robust domestic demand. Imports have increased at a rapid clip despite President Donald Trump's aggressive tariffs.

Trump has defended the duties as necessary to shrink the trade gap and rejuvenate the nation's industrial base. 

The Trump administration this week proposed new maximum potential rates of 20 per cent to 40 per cent on 14 major trading partners including China, Japan ​and the European Union, to counter what the White House said was excess industrial capacity that these countries are promoting.

"The trade deficit in goods worsened in October, which will take a toll on economic growth in the fourth quarter," said Christopher Rupkey, chief economist at FwdBonds. "Capital goods imports are surging, showing that AI doesn't always lead to greater US economic growth."

The goods trade shortfall jumped 10.7 per cent, or US$14.4 billion (S$18.6 billion), to US$149.5 billion last month, the highest level since March 2025, the Commerce Department's Census Bureau said. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast the goods deficit at US$133 billion.

Goods imports shot up 6.1 per cent, or US$21.1 billion, to US$365.3 billion, the highest level since the government started tracking the series in 1992. The broad increase in imports was led by capital goods, which soared 8.5 per cent. Capital goods increased 80.0 per cent on a year-on-year basis in October.

Businesses are aggressively spending on AI, giving the technology a prominent role in the economy. But the AI infrastructure buildout is heavily reliant on imports, which are a subtraction from gross domestic product growth.

Imports of consumer goods advanced 2.6 per cent while those of other goods increased 4.5 per cent. Domestic demand, which includes business investment and consumer spending, grew in the third quarter at its fastest pace in more than five years.

Imports of industrial supplies, which include crude oil and nonmonetary gold, increased 6.0 per cent last month, while those of motor vehicles, engines and parts accelerated 4.1 per cent. Imports of foods, feeds and beverages rose 2.5 per cent.

AI adding less to GDP growth

"This year's surge in capital goods imports is one reason why AI is adding less to GDP than corporate spending figures suggest," economists at Goldman Sachs wrote in a note.

Exports of goods increased 3.2 per cent, or US$6.7 billion, to US$215.8 billion. Exports of industrial supplies advanced 4.9 per cent and shipments of capital goods rose 3.4 per cent.

Exports of motor vehicles, engines and parts vaulted 5.7 per cent, while those of consumer goods increased 4.2 per cent. But exports of foods, feeds and beverages slumped 7.9 per cent.

The government reported on Wednesday that trade sliced off 3.21 percentage points from GDP growth in the third quarter. 

The drag was, however, more than offset by robust growth in consumer spending and business investment in equipment, mostly AI-related. The economy grew at a 4.3 per cent annualised rate last quarter after expanding at a 2.2 per cent pace in the April-June period.

Trade has not contributed to gross domestic product growth for four straight quarters, reflecting strong domestic demand.

The anticipated hit to GDP growth from trade this quarter could be blunted by businesses rebuilding inventories to meet demand.

The Census Bureau also reported on Friday that wholesale inventories increased 0.9 per cent in October after rising 0.8 per cent in September. Stocks at wholesalers were lifted by a 1.6 per cent jump in durable goods inventories. 

Retail inventories increased 0.8 per cent after climbing 0.7 per cent in September. Stocks at motor vehicle and parts dealers jumped 1.3 per cent after rising 0.6 per cent in September.

Excluding motor vehicles and parts, retail inventories increased 0.6 per cent last month after gaining 0.7 per cent in September. This component goes into the calculation of GDP.

Inventory investment rebounded in the third quarter after declining for five straight quarters. It added 1.64 percentage points to GDP growth last quarter.

Economists at Goldman Sachs lowered their fourth-quarter GDP growth estimate by 0.2 percentage point to a 2.2 per cent rate. This estimate also factored in October's wholesale and inventory data, which they said partly offset the drag from the large trade deficit.

Source: Reuters

data.title: Oil notches first weekly gain in November on supply fears
data.description:
HOUSTON — Brent crude edged down on Friday (Nov 27), but snapped a three-week losing streak to notch its first weekly gain in November, as attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz and Saudi energy infrastructure fanned concerns over Middle East supplies.

Brent crude futures fell US$1.13 (S$1.46), or 1.2 per cent, to US$95.44 a barrel. It hit its highest since Nov 9 earlier in the session, but stayed shy of the US$100 mark.

US West Texas Intermediate crude futures settled at US$83.08 a barrel, down 60 cents, or 0.7 per cent, from Wednesday's close. There was no Thursday settlement for WTI because of the US Thanksgiving holiday.

Brent gained about three per cent on the week, while WTI lost 0.9 per cent.

"Attacks on Middle Eastern energy facilities and tankers have brought supply disruption back into focus," said Mark Schaefer, a director at brokerage Liquidity Energy.

Prices retreated in recent weeks as investors were relieved that US President Donald Trump did not step up military action against Iran after the midterm elections.

However, Iran has continued to attack ships transiting the key Strait of Hormuz, disrupting oil exports, while Yemen's Houthis have struck Saudi Arabian infrastructure.

The US military said on Friday it disabled a commercial ship on Thursday after it attempted to run the US blockade of Iran, while an adviser to the Iranian supreme leader said Iran would keep the Strait of Hormuz shut while vowing to break the embargo.

Saudi Aramco's Jazan refinery temporarily halted some operations after a projectile struck it on Thursday, killing a worker, Saudi Arabia's Energy Ministry said.

The strike was the latest blow to key Saudi facilities, a day after the Houthis claimed attacks on Ras Tanura, the kingdom's largest refinery and a major crude export hub.

OPEC+, which includes Saudi Arabia and Russia, is set to keep first-quarter 2027 output targets unchanged when the group meets on Sunday, three people with knowledge of the talks said.

Separately, 10 people familiar with the matter told Reuters that the US administration encouraged Venezuela and Iraq to consider leaving OPEC earlier this year and blocked Venezuela from paying its membership dues.

Iraq is in negotiations with OPEC to raise its production ceiling as the country looks to develop its energy sector, oil minister Basim Mohammed Khudair said on Friday ahead of the OPEC+ meeting.

"We think Brent can still push above US$100 a barrel without another major escalation in the Middle East, but that increasingly requires evidence of constrained deliverable supply," ANZ analysts Brian Martin and Daniel Hynes said in a research note.

Ukraine has intensified drone attacks on Russian oil refineries since the end of October, with the latest incident causing a fire at the Slavyansk ECO refinery in Russia's southern region of Krasnodar.

Separately, fires disrupted activity at Thailand's Bangchak refinery and Venezuela's Amuay refinery on Thursday.

Source: Reuters

data.title: AirAsia delays staff salary payments to end of month, internal email shows
data.description:
HONG KONG/KUALA LUMPUR — AirAsia has told employees it will delay salary payments to the end of each month from November through March, according to an internal email seen by Reuters, as the airline takes measures to conserve cash and its Philippine unit cuts jobs.

The email, sent to Malaysia-based staff late last week by Chief People Officer Muhammad Khurram Zia, cited the need for a "temporary operational adjustment" at Southeast Asia's largest budget airline, which like its peers faces higher jet fuel costs.

Salary payments during the five-month period would be made on the 30th of each month or the last day of February, the email said.

It cited a "challenging environment" and asked employees for "patience and flexibility".

The email's contents were confirmed by two people familiar with the matter. One of the people said AirAsia had previously paid salaries earlier in the second half of each month.

AirAsia did not respond to a request for comment.

The Iran war has sent jet fuel prices soaring, putting airlines worldwide under their worst financial strain since the Covid-19 pandemic.

US low-cost carrier Spirit Airlines collapsed in May, Latvia's airBaltic sought bankruptcy protection in September and Norway's Norse Atlantic suspended flights on Thursday as it looks for urgent short-term financing.

AirAsia Philippines announces layoffs

Shares in AirAsia, which employs about 26,000 people predominantly in Asia, have declined more than 70 per cent this year as elevated fuel prices and foreign exchange losses squeezed its operations.

AirAsia Philippines said on Thursday it would reduce its workforce following sustained pressure on its operating costs, without specifying how many staff would be affected.

The airline said on Friday it remained fully operational and committed to serving the Philippine market. The planned workforce adjustment will not affect passenger flights, booking or other services, AirAsia Philippines General Manager and President Anna Victoria Lu said in a statement.

The AirAsia Philippines Pilots' Union filed notice of a strike after 90 pilots were retrenched, its president said in a video posted on social media on Thursday.

Philippine Labor Secretary Francis Tolentino confirmed receiving notice in a text message to Reuters.

AirAsia reported its third consecutive quarterly loss on Monday, though it was narrower than the prior quarter. Its cash and bank balances stood at 905 million ringgit (S$283 million) as of Sept 30, down five per cent from June 30.

In an investor presentation accompanying its results, the airline said it was taking measures to conserve cash, including suspending unviable routes and returning 25 planes to lessors.

It said more planes could exit its fleet in 2027, and a creditor restructuring was underway as part of a plan to reset the business before rebuilding in 2028.

AirAsia CEO Bo Lingam said on Monday that the third-quarter results suggested "the worst is behind us", while cautioning that fourth-quarter fuel costs were expected to rise further.

Malaysia's government has been weighing options to support AirAsia without putting public funds at risk, Reuters has previously reported.

The country's finance ministry said on Thursday that it would ask AirAsia for priority over other lenders and strengthen oversight of the airline's board and management if it decided to extend support.

data.title: Bank of Japan calls for safeguards against digital money, AI risks
data.description:
TOKYO — Global policymakers must strengthen defences against financial stability and cybersecurity risks posed by the emergence of new forms of digital money and financial infrastructure, Bank of Japan Executive Director Kazushige Kamiyama said on Friday (Nov 27).

New forms of digital money, such as stablecoins and tokenised deposits, are likely to co-exist and interact, which poses fresh challenges for policymakers such as ensuring the diversity does not create unnecessary fragmentation or undermine financial stability, he said.

The growing use of AI also brings fresh cybersecurity risks, requiring authorities and institutions to strengthen their defences against the growing ability of AI to discover and exploit vulnerabilities, Kamiyama said.

"My central message is that technological innovation offers significant opportunities to improve money and payments, but innovation must go hand in hand with trust," Kamiyama said in a speech at the International Monetary Fund's seminar on digital money and payments in Tokyo.

"Central bank money will continue to play a fundamental role as the anchor of trust in the monetary system," he said.

Tokenisation is the process of turning assets such as bonds, deposits and securities into digital tokens that can be traded and settled on programmable platforms.

Policymakers globally are increasingly moving beyond experiments toward establishing rules and infrastructure for wider use, while seeking to ensure tokenised finance remains in the realm of regulated money and traditional financial system.

By creating new channels of trading across institutions and markets, tokenisation may amplify market movements during times of stress, Kamiyama said, citing it among risks that warrant vigilance.

Interconnected platforms may also allow cyber incidents to spread quickly, meaning new platforms must be designed with security and resilience from the outset, he said.

Beyond technological challenges, policymakers must create legal frameworks to clarify whether the transfer of a token effectively transfers legal rights and obligations in the underlying asset, Kamiyama said.

"Taken together, these challenges show that the benefits of tokenisation depend not on technology alone, but also on sound institutional arrangements, clear legal frameworks, and public-private co-operation," he said.

Source: Reuters

data.title: Oil on track to snap 3-week losing streak over supply fears
data.description:
SINGAPORE — Oil prices rose slightly on Friday (Nov 27) and are on track to snap a three-week losing streak as ongoing attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz and Saudi energy infrastructure heightened concerns over oil supply from the conflict-hit Middle East.

Brent crude futures rose four cents to US$96.61 (S$125) a barrel by 4.50am GMT (12.50pm SGT), after gaining nearly US$2 on Thursday to settle at their highest since Nov 6.

US West Texas Intermediate crude futures were at US$85.78 a barrel, up US$2.10, or 2.5 per cent, from their close on Wednesday. There was no settlement for WTI on Thursday due to the Thanksgiving holiday in the US.

"We think Brent can still push above USD100/bbl without another major escalation in the Middle East, but that increasingly requires evidence of constrained deliverable supply," ANZ analysts Brian Martin and Daniel Hynes said in a note.

Prices slipped in previous weeks on relief that US President Donald Trump did not step up military action on Iran after the midterm elections. However, Iran has continued to attack ships transiting the Hormuz strait, disrupting oil exports, while Yemeni Houthis have struck Saudi infrastructure.

"Recovering Gulf exports and easing geopolitical risk support lower oil prices in 2027. However, depleted inventories, persistent shipping risks and slow refinery repairs leave the market exposed," OCBC analyst Sim Moh Siong said in a note.

Saudi Aramco's Jazan refinery temporarily halted some operations after a projectile struck the facility on Thursday, killing a Nepalese worker and wounding several others, Saudi Arabia's Energy Ministry said in a statement.

The strike was the Houthis' latest blow against key Saudi facilities, a day after the group claimed attacks on Ras Tanura, the kingdom's largest refinery and a major crude export hub, and the Red Sea ports of Jeddah and Jazan, amid escalating hostilities between the two sides.

Given the disruption from the Iran war, OPEC+ is likely to maintain its oil output targets for at least the first quarter of 2027 at a meeting on Sunday, two sources said.

Meanwhile, Ukraine has intensified drone attacks on Russian oil refineries since the end of October, with the latest incident causing a fire at the Slavyansk ECO refinery in Russia's southern Krasnodar region.

Separately, fires disrupted activity at Thailand's Bangchak refinery and Venezuela's Amuay refinery on Thursday.

Source: Reuters

data.title: Caltex mirrors Shell, Sinopec and Esso to drop petrol prices in second round of reductions
data.description:
Chevron-owned Caltex has become the fourth major fuel company here to drop petrol prices in the second round of price reductions.

In a price board update published at 11am on Friday (Nov 27), Caltex announced a four-cent drop across its 92-, 95-octane and premium petrol offerings, while keeping the price of its diesel unchanged.

This mirrors moves made by Shell and Sinopec on Nov 25, and later, Esso on Nov 26.

As with the three other major fuel companies, this is also the second reduction for Caltex since Sept 14, when fuel prices first rose again after over two months of unchanged prices.

Its last three-cent per litre reduction across its petrol and diesel offerings was recorded on Nov 4.

SPC has not raised prices since Oct 16, electing not to join the round of price hikes recorded between Oct 29 and Nov 2.

Following the latest round of price adjustments, the price of the more popular 95-octane petrol at major fuel companies is at $3.56 across all five major retailers — Caltex, Esso, Shell, Sinopec and SPC.

Meanwhile, Union Gas-owned Cnergy and Smart Energy are offering the petrol grade at $2.50 and $2.58 respectively.

An oil tanker hit a naval mine and caught fire in a "restricted zone" in the strait on Wednesday, the semi-official Fars news agency cited the Iranian Army as saying in a statement.

data.title: Necessities join gifts in Black Friday shopping carts as AI and higher costs steer spending
data.description:
NEW YORK — Stocking up on discounted shampoo while grabbing a flat-screen TV and several Lego sets for under the tree. Making a holiday list, comparing style options and delivery dates, and finding the best price with help from artificial intelligence.

Black Friday, the retail industry's version of the Super Bowl, comes with a few twists this year. Brands and stores have promoted steep discounts online and in stores all month, making the day once considered the holiday shopping season's unofficial kickoff seem more like the fourth quarter of a football game.

AI-powered shopping tools and cost concerns fuelled by the US war with Iran also are influencing how, where, when and on what consumers are spending, according to industry analysts. 

When Black Friday deals are available, basics like T-shirts, toiletries and pet supplies are going into shopping carts along with gift items, analysts said.

"Usually, when you think of holiday shopping, it's premium handbags and jewellery and those types of items, but we're fast seeing shoppers also use this season to stock up on the essentials," said Vivek Pandya, director of digital insights at technology company Adobe.

Black Friday still has enough die-hard traditionalists to make it the biggest day of the year for retail foot traffic, according to Sensormatic Solutions, which tracks activity at physical stores. 

Retailers large and small view the occasion as an opportunity to improve their year-end footing and to attract new customers.

"Black Friday is still the day for in-store shopping," Grant Gustafson, Sensormatic's head of retail consulting and analytics, said.

This year's holiday shopping takes place in a US economic environment marked by lackluster consumer confidence, high inflation and shoppers who have kept spending regardless. 

Foot traffic data show Americans are visiting stores less often this season, and their purchases appear more intentional than impulse-driven, Gustafson said.

Here are some of the emerging trends for Black Friday and holiday shopping overall in 2026:

Online spending so far has exceeded expectations

Analysts and economists closely scrutinize retail spending on the five days that begin with Thanksgiving Day and end on Cyber Monday for clues about consumers' financial staying power and retailers' prospects during the crucial holiday period and into the new year.

The good news for retailers is that consumer confidence jumped this month as US gasoline prices continued a steady decline.

Online sales have beaten expectations so far this holiday season, according to Adobe Digital Insights, a research and market intelligence programme that Pandya leads. US consumers spent US$82.5 billion (S$106.3 billion) online from Nov 1 to Nov 22, 9.1 per cent more than during the same three weeks last year.

Adobe predicted that US online sales for the holiday shopping season that runs through Dec 31 would grow by 6.7 per cent and total US$275.1 billion. 

The National Retail Federation estimated that higher prices would account for about half of the 4.1 per cent sales growth it expected in stores and online in November and December. The group forecast US shoppers collectively spending US$1.01 trillion.

Thanksgiving Day and Black Friday still might have bigger discounts

US retailers have broadly held the line on prices instead of making big increases across the board, and offered solid discounts that persuaded customers to shop earlier, industry analysts said.

Technology company Salesforce, which tracks digital spending at a range of retailers, including grocery stores, said November discounts are eight per cent bigger than last year. 

The seasonal promotions pushed average selling prices of physical merchandise one per cent below last November's prices, Salesforce said.

Caila Schwartz, a retail and consumer insights leader at Salesforce, said the discounts encouraged shoppers to add two per cent more items in their online carts from Oct 1 through Nov 18 compared with the same period a year ago.

"In the last several years, a lot of the (sales) gains have been from higher prices," she said. "This is not what we are seeing this year."

While retailers offered discounts earlier this year, with some starting before Halloween, Adobe's Pandya said the best prices still are likely to land on Thanksgiving and Black Friday.

For example, discounts on TVs are expected to average 23 per cent on Friday compared with 11 per cent during the first 22 days of the month.

Shoppers are buying household items along with holiday gifts

Self-gifting is an established holiday shopping trend. Black Friday's expansion to a multiweek event also has some consumers filling their cupboards with toiletries and clothes they would typically buy at another time, according to analysts.

Online sales of personal hygiene products were 40 per cent higher from Nov 1 through Nov 22 compared to the October average, according to Adobe's data. Sales of household cleaning products spiked 33 per cent and clothing basics by 27 per cent during the same time frame, Adobe said.

The deepest holiday discounts are expected on clothing, home goods, and health and beauty, Salesforce said. The company said it expected health and beauty products to average 33 per cent off between Tuesday and next Monday.

"It's not just a moment where shoppers are buying gifts," Schwartz said. "They're also buying things that they need, and so that's going to help drive up a lot of the spend."

AI tools may be persuading users to do more online shopping

Consumers are using AI-assisted tools to help them compare products and prices, particularly as inflation and paying more for gasoline has made them more attuned to price tags, Pandya said.

A belief that e-commerce sites will offer "the best value possible" has contributed to shoppers doing more of their holiday period spending online instead of in stores, he said.

Traffic to online retail sites from links in AI-powered tools more than doubled this month compared with November 2025, Adobe said.

Walmart CEO John Furner told analysts during an earnings call this month that customers who employed Sparky, the retailer's AI shopping assistant, spent 40 per cent more per order on average than shoppers who did not use the tool.

Amazon CEO Andy Jassy told analysts last month that US shoppers using its AI assistant Alexa spend 50 per cent more than those who don't.

Source: Associated Press

data.title: Argentina bans its central bank from printing money for the government
data.description:
BUENOS AIRES, Argentina — Argentina's Congress voted Thursday (Nov 26) to bar the central bank from printing money to pay the government's bills, enshrining in law a key pillar of President Javier Milei's fight against the country's notoriously high inflation.

Under the new charter, the central bank's "primary and fundamental mission" will be to preserve the value of the peso — a goal Milei has pursued in office even though, as a candidate in 2023, he promised to abolish the bank and replace the local currency with the US dollar.

The 141-0 vote in the Chamber of Deputies, with 99 abstentions, comes days after preliminary figures showed Argentina had likely slipped into recession, less than a year before the libertarian economist seeks a second four-year term.

For generations, when Argentine governments spent more than they collected in taxes, they turned to the central bank to print pesos to fill the gap, fueling repeated currency crises and bouts of hyperinflation. 

The law puts an end to "91 years of plunder, expropriation, impunity and institutional decay", Milei's office said in a statement.

The new charter bars the bank from lending to any level of government or otherwise financing the Treasury. It also scraps the bank's employment and economic development goals added under former President Cristina Fernández de Kirchner, the Peronist opposition leader whose administrations leaned heavily on the central bank to fund unbridled spending.

But the law gives the monetary authority less protection than Milei sought. His original bill would have required a two-thirds vote in both houses of Congress to remove the bank's governor, his appointee Santiago Bausili. 

The Senate watered down that clause, and the lower house lacked the votes Thursday to restore it. Now a president can replace the bank's leadership with a simple Senate majority.

Milei has slashed public spending in the past three years, turning Argentina's chronic fiscal deficits into a surplus and helping cut annual inflation from nearly 300 per cent in early 2024 to 33 per cent last month.

Yet Milei has been reluctant to let the market set Argentina's most important price: the exchange rate. The charter leaves currency controls in the bank's hands and sets no clear rule for how it should respond to inflation.

Tight monetary policy has kept the peso strong, making Argentine goods expensive abroad just as factories face a flood of cheaper imports. Oil and gas exports have boomed while labour-intensive industries like manufacturing, retail and construction have struggled.

Argentina's economy shrank an estimated 1.8 per cent in the third quarter, after a 0.6 per cent contraction in the second, according to official data released Tuesday. Two straight quarters of decline is the usual definition of a recession.

As Milei's support slips in the polls, investors wary of a country infamous for defaulting on its debt nine times are weighing the possibility that the Peronists — the populist movement that has long dominated Argentine politics — could return to power and reverse his market-friendly reforms. 

The premium investors demand to hold Argentina's bonds, a gauge of perceived default risk, has more than doubled since early August, according to JPMorgan.

Under growing pressure, Milei is now hoping to overhaul next year's presidential race. The Senate on Thursday approved his bill to suspend the mandatory primaries, which the government argues waste public money on contests parties should run themselves. It now goes to the lower house for a vote.

Suspending the primaries, long a bellwether for the general election, would spare Milei an early verdict from voters — one that, if poor, could spook markets and sink the peso and his support with it.

Peronist leaders have balked at the move, which would force their fractured movement to negotiate a ticket behind closed doors or scramble to organise a primary of its own.

"Milei now wants to change the rules of democracy to improve his chances of reelection by cheating," Buenos Aires province Gov. Axel Kicillof, a potential Peronist challenger to Milei, wrote on X.

Source: Associated Press

data.title: Viettel, Singtel start building submarine cable linking Vietnam, Singapore and Thailand
data.description:
HANOI — Vietnam's military-run telecoms group Viettel on Thursday (Nov 26) said it had started construction with Singapore Telecommunications, or Singtel, of a new submarine cable linking Vietnam, Thailand and Singapore.

The Vietnam-Thailand-Singapore cable will stretch about 2,500 km and have a design capacity of 600 terabits per second (Tbps), with a completion target of the fourth quarter of 2030, Viettel said in a statement

The Vietnam-Singapore section alone will have a capacity of 240 Tbps, about 2.5 times the combined capacity of Vietnam's currently operating international cable systems

Other partners in the project include Vietnam's VNPT and FPT Telecom and Thailand's AIS, it said

Japan's NEC Corp and Singapore-based ASEAN Cableship are the project's contractors

Viettel currently participates in five of Vietnam's eight international submarine cable systems and carries around 65 per cent of the country's international connectivity capacity, it said

The group aims to be involved in about 10 international cable systems by 2030, including routes designed and led by Vietnamese firms.

Source: Reuters
